title: The Room Behind the Office
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 10 of 40
content:
I learned about the room behind Snape's office because he fell asleep at his desk.

Again, this sounds simpler than it was.

Severus Snape did not drift gently into sleep.

He lost a fight with consciousness.

One moment he was correcting a Ministry inventory form with the vicious concentration of a man personally offended by bureaucratic grammar. The next, his quill stopped moving.

His head lowered by an inch.

Then another.

He jerked awake.

“I am working.”

“I didn't say anything.”

“You were about to.”

“I was about to ask whether powdered armadillo bile should be listed as biological or alchemical stock.”

“Biological.”

His eyes closed.

I waited.

They opened.

“Go to bed,” I said.

“No.”

“Excellent talk.”

I returned to my own forms.

Five minutes later, his quill drew a long black line across the parchment as his hand went slack.

This time he did not wake.

I sat very still.

There are moments when another person's trust is obvious. A secret offered. A confession. A hand deliberately extended.

Then there are moments like that one.

Snape asleep in front of me.

No wand in hand. No expression arranged. No awareness of the door.

It felt more private than the memory vials.

I stood quietly and went to fetch a blanket from the camp bed behind his desk.

Except the camp bed was gone.

The wall behind it stood slightly open.

I frowned.

A narrow door had been concealed in the stone.

Rule two: no entering his office without permission.

I was already in the office. He had invited me hours ago to help with paperwork.

Rule two was annoyingly unspecific about secret doors.

I considered waking him.

Then he shivered.

The dungeon was cold.

I opened the hidden door just enough to look for a blanket.

A small room lay beyond.

Not a bedroom exactly.

A refuge.

There was a narrow bed with plain dark covers, a wardrobe, a washstand, and two shelves of books. A kettle sat on a small stove. One chair faced a fireplace no larger than a cabinet.

Everything was neat.

Everything was worn.

Nothing looked new except a jar of healing salve on the washstand.

I found a folded wool blanket at the foot of the bed.

I took it and closed the door.

Snape woke while I was draping it over the back of his chair.

His wand appeared under my chin.

I froze.

His eyes were wild for half a second.

Then recognition arrived.

The wand dropped.

“What are you doing?”

His voice was hoarse with sleep and alarm.

“Trying not to let you freeze.”

His gaze moved to the blanket.

Then to the hidden door.

His face hardened.

“You went in there.”

“One step.”

“You had no permission.”

“You were asleep.”

“That does not suspend the concept of privacy.”

“No.”

I set the blanket on the chair.

“You're right.”

The immediate agreement seemed to disorient him.

“I should have woken you,” I said. “I didn't want to. I made the wrong choice.”

He stared at me.

I did not explain further.

I did not say I had meant well.

Intent did not erase the boundary.

“I am sorry.”

The anger in his face did not disappear, but it changed shape.

“You saw the room.”

“Yes.”

“What else?”

“A bed. Books. A kettle. A wardrobe.”

His eyes narrowed.

“The washstand?”

“Yes.”

“The photographs?”

“There were no photographs that I noticed.”

He searched my face.

I understood then that there probably were photographs. Hidden, maybe inside the wardrobe or a drawer. Things he had expected me to discover if I were nosy enough.

“I didn't open anything,” I said.

He sat back.

For a moment, exhaustion won over anger.

He looked old.

Not elderly. Worn.

There was a difference.

“I slept there during the war,” he said.

I waited.

“When leaving the office became… impractical.”

Because the Carrows watched him? Because Voldemort summoned him at all hours? Because children might need protection? Because he had been afraid to go home?

I had a dozen questions.

I asked none.

Snape rubbed a hand over his face.

“You may take the blanket.”

“I don't need it.”

“Then why did you invade a private room to acquire it?”

“For you.”

His hand stopped.

“You were cold.”

The silence that followed was so complete I heard water ticking somewhere in the pipes.

At last he said, “I am not accustomed to being monitored while unconscious.”

“That is one way to make sleeping sound criminal.”

His mouth twitched, then flattened.

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

He looked at the blanket.

Then pulled it over his knees with an expression of profound irritation.

I returned to my chair.

Neither of us mentioned the wand under my chin.

I suspected he was waiting for me to be frightened.

I was.

A little.

Not of him in the way I might once have been. Of reflexes built deeply enough that waking meant arming himself before knowing where he was.

“You should sleep properly,” I said.

His eyes sharpened.

“Careful.”

“Rule three. No amateur psychology before noon. It's after midnight.”

He glanced at the clock.

“An unfortunate loophole.”

“I'm exploiting it.”

“Of course you are.”

I set down my quill.

“Why don't you?”

“Why don't I what?”

“Sleep.”

He looked toward the hidden door.

“I do.”

“That was technically an answer.”

He did not respond.

I leaned back.

“Fine. My turn.”

His brow furrowed.

“I don't sleep well in new places,” I said. “First week anywhere, I wake up at every sound. Hogwarts has approximately nine thousand sounds per hour.”

“There are quieter rooms.”

“Mine is beneath a portrait of a wizard who snores.”

“Portraits do not require oxygen.”

“Tell him that.”

Snape looked amused despite himself.

“I've been using a silencing charm,” I continued. “Then I wake up because it's too quiet.”

“That is idiotic.”

“Yes.”

“Why are you telling me?”

“Because asking you to talk about sleep while pretending mine is simple would be unfair.”

His gaze stayed on me.

“You think reciprocity creates permission.”

“No. I think it creates honesty.”

He considered that.

Then he looked down at his hands.

“I wake when the mark burns.”

I went still.

The Dark Mark.

“But Voldemort is dead.”

“I am aware.”

“Does it still—”

“No. Not physically.”

I understood.

Dreams could reproduce sensations with obscene accuracy.

“And the shack?” I asked softly.

His fingers touched his throat.

“Sometimes.”

I nodded.

No pity.

No promise.

“What helps?”

His expression turned sardonic.

“Exhaustion.”

“That is not treatment.”

“No. It is effective.”

“Until you fall asleep over Ministry forms.”

“A merciful alternative to reading them awake.”

I laughed.

He looked almost pleased.

We abandoned the paperwork.

I brewed tea in the small kettle from his hidden room, with permission this time. The tea was better than the pub's and worse than I expected from someone so exacting about Potions.

I told him so.

“Tea is not a potion.”

“That sounds like cowardice.”

“It is a beverage.”

“A badly brewed one.”

He took the cup from my hand, tasted it, and frowned.

“You oversteeped it.”

“You told me four minutes.”

“I said three.”

“You whispered.”

“You failed to listen.”

“Your throat is injured.”

“Your ears are not.”

The argument carried us to one in the morning.

At some point, Snape's shoulders lowered.

At some point, I stopped listening for the castle's noises.

When I finally stood to leave, he folded the blanket and set it on the desk.

“Keep it,” I said.

“It is mine.”

“Exactly.”

He gave me a strange look.

At the door, I paused.

“Good night, Snape.”

His expression shifted.

“Good night.”

It was the first time the words had passed between us.

Walking back to my quarters, I realized the castle sounded different.

Not quieter.

Before I stood, my attention caught on the shelf beside his chair. It held fewer books than the office outside and stranger things between them: a cracked chess piece, a tiny brass scale, two unopened letters, a corked vial of beach-colored sand.

I pointed at the sand. “That seems suspiciously decorative.”

“It is not decoration.”

“What is it?”

“Sand.”

“I had gathered that.”

His expression suggested I was testing the limits of mercy.

After a pause he said, “A sample from Tunisia. There are mineral traces useful in certain glassmaking charms.”

“You kept souvenir sand for research.”

“I kept a material sample.”

“Of course.”

I looked around the small hidden room again. It did not feel like the lair of a secretive villain. It felt like the place of someone who had never expected to be known and had therefore built privacy in layers.

“Do many people know this room exists?”

“Fewer than three.”

“That's an ominous way to say two.”

“One is a portrait.”

I laughed.

His mouth moved, almost smiling.

The room was still private after I had seen it. That mattered. Being invited inside did not make me its owner.

Less empty.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
